acceptedAnswer.text: TreeSet is a class in java.util that implements the NavigableSet interface and is backed by a Red-Black Tree (via TreeMap internally). It stores elements in sorted ascending order (natural ordering or custom Comparator), does not allow duplicate elements, does not allow null elements, and provides O(log n) time complexity for add, remove, and contains operations.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between TreeSet and HashSet?

acceptedAnswer.text: HashSet uses hashing (backed by HashMap) — O(1) average operations, no guaranteed order, allows one null element. TreeSet uses a Red-Black Tree (backed by TreeMap) — O(log n) operations, always sorted in natural or Comparator order, does not allow null elements. Use HashSet for fast membership testing; use TreeSet when sorted iteration or range queries (ceiling, floor, headSet, tailSet) are needed.

No. TreeSet does not allow null elements. Adding null to a TreeSet throws a NullPointerException because TreeSet must compare elements to maintain sorted order, and calling compareTo() or compare() on null causes a NullPointerException. HashSet and LinkedHashSet allow one null element, but TreeSet strictly prohibits it.

mainEntity.name: What is the internal data structure of TreeSet?

acceptedAnswer.text: TreeSet is backed internally by a TreeMap. Every element added to a TreeSet is stored as a key in the backing TreeMap, with a constant dummy value (PRESENT). TreeMap itself is implemented as a Red-Black Tree — a self-balancing binary search tree that guarantees O(log n) time for add, remove, and contains operations and always maintains elements in sorted order.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between ceiling(), floor(), higher(), and lower() in TreeSet?

acceptedAnswer.text: floor(e) returns the greatest element less than or equal to e (includes e). lower(e) returns the greatest element strictly less than e (excludes e). ceiling(e) returns the smallest element greater than or equal to e (includes e). higher(e) returns the smallest element strictly greater than e (excludes e). All return null if no such element exists.

blocks.text: TreeSet is a class in the java.util package that implements the NavigableSet interface, which extends SortedSet, which extends Set. It is backed internally by a TreeMap, which itself is a Red-Black Tree — a self-balancing binary search tree. This makes TreeSet the go-to choice whenever you need a collection of unique elements in always-sorted order.

TreeSet guarantees that its elements are always stored in ascending order — either the natural order defined by the element's Comparable implementation, or a custom order defined by a Comparator supplied at construction time. Every add(), remove(), and contains() operation runs in O(log n) time — slower than HashSet's O(1) average, but TreeSet offers something HashSet cannot: sorted iteration and powerful range queries.

Three critical rules define TreeSet behavior: (1) No duplicate elements — duplicates are silently ignored. (2) No null elements — adding null throws NullPointerException. (3) Elements must be mutually comparable — adding an incompatible type throws ClassCastException.
Understanding the full interface hierarchy of TreeSet explains why it has such a rich API — it inherits methods from multiple interfaces all the way up to Iterable.

sections.title: Internal Working of TreeSet — Red-Black Tree

blocks.text: TreeSet is internally backed by a TreeMap. Every element you add to a TreeSet is stored as a key in the backing TreeMap, with a constant dummy value (PRESENT = new Object()). This means TreeSet reuses all of TreeMap's Red-Black Tree machinery.
A Red-Black Tree is a self-balancing Binary Search Tree (BST) that maintains the following five invariants to guarantee O(log n) height:

items.text: — Every node is either RED or BLACK.
— The root node is always BLACK.
— All null leaf nodes (NIL sentinels) are considered BLACK.
— A RED node cannot have a RED parent or RED child (no two consecutive red nodes on any path).
— Every path from a node to its descendant null leaves contains the same number of BLACK nodes.

blocks.text: These invariants together guarantee the tree height is always at most 2 × log₂(n+1), which bounds all operations at O(log n). When add() or remove() violates these properties, the tree performs rotations and recoloring — invisible to the developer — to restore balance automatically.

Why does this matter for you as a developer? Unlike HashSet where worst-case performance degrades to O(n) with a poor hash function, TreeSet's O(log n) guarantee is unconditional — no hash collisions, no load factor resizing, no surprises. For 1 million elements, log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20 — TreeSet finds any element in at most ~20 comparisons.

blocks.text: TreeSet is NOT thread-safe. Concurrent access by multiple threads without external synchronization can corrupt the underlying Red-Black Tree structure, causing infinite loops, incorrect results, or ConcurrentModificationException. Java provides several approaches to use TreeSet safely in multi-threaded environments:

blocks.label: Thread-Safe TreeSet — Three Approaches
lines: public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
// Simple wrapper — all methods synchronized on the set object
// IMPORTANT: manual synchronization needed during iteration
// Best for concurrent sorted set — lock-free, thread-safe
// Use ReentrantReadWriteLock for max performance under high reads
// (pattern used in production systems — see java.util.concurrent.locks)

blocks.text: Recommendation: For thread-safe sorted sets in modern Java applications, prefer ConcurrentSkipListSet over Collections.synchronizedSortedSet(new TreeSet<>()). ConcurrentSkipListSet uses a lock-free skip list that provides better concurrency than a single synchronized mutex on the entire set, and still guarantees sorted order and O(log n) operations.

blocks.text: Practice This Code — Live Editor
TreeSet is a highly specialized collection. Understanding its strengths and limitations helps you use it in exactly the right situations.

pros.title: Always Sorted
pros.text: Elements are automatically maintained in sorted order after every add or remove. No need to sort manually — saving development effort and preventing bugs.

pros.title: Guaranteed O(log n) Performance
pros.text: Unlike HashSet where worst-case degrades with hash collisions, TreeSet's Red-Black Tree guarantees O(log n) for all operations unconditionally — predictable performance at any scale.

pros.title: Rich NavigableSet API
pros.text: ceiling(), floor(), higher(), lower(), pollFirst(), pollLast(), descendingSet() — these proximity and navigation methods are exclusive to TreeSet and enable complex algorithms with minimal code.

pros.title: Powerful Range Views
pros.text: headSet(), tailSet(), subSet() return live backed views — ideal for range queries, time-window processing, price bands, and interval lookups without creating copies.

pros.title: Custom Ordering via Comparator
pros.text: Any sort order is possible — by length, by frequency, by custom business rules. Pass a Comparator to the constructor and TreeSet handles the rest.

pros.title: No Duplicates Guaranteed
pros.text: TreeSet enforces element uniqueness automatically. Ideal for deduplicating data when sorted order also matters.

pros.title: Java 21 SequencedSet Support
pros.text: getFirst(), getLast(), reversed(), removeFirst(), removeLast() — clean first/last access without the verbose workarounds needed before Java 21.

cons.title: Slower than HashSet
cons.text: O(log n) per operation vs O(1) average for HashSet. For large datasets where order doesn't matter, HashSet is significantly faster.

cons.title: No Null Elements
cons.text: Adding null throws NullPointerException because compareTo(null) fails. Use HashSet or LinkedHashSet if null elements are needed.

cons.title: Higher Memory per Node
cons.text: Each Red-Black Tree node stores the element plus references to left child, right child, parent, and a color bit — more overhead per element than a HashMap bucket entry.

cons.title: Not Thread-Safe
cons.text: TreeSet is not synchronized. Multi-threaded use without external synchronization corrupts the tree. Use ConcurrentSkipListSet for concurrent sorted sets.

cons.title: Elements Must Be Comparable
cons.text: Without a Comparator, elements must implement Comparable. Adding incompatible types (e.g., mixing String and Integer) throws ClassCastException at runtime.

cons.title: Live Views Can Surprise You
cons.text: headSet(), tailSet(), and subSet() return live backed views. Structural modifications to one affect the other — this is powerful but can cause unexpected behavior if you are not careful.

blocks.text: These are the most frequently asked TreeSet interview questions for Java developer positions — from fresher to senior level. Master all of them.

items.q: Q1. What is TreeSet in Java and how is it different from HashSet?
items.a: TreeSet is a Set implementation backed by a Red-Black Tree (via TreeMap) that stores elements in sorted ascending order, with O(log n) operations, and no null elements allowed. HashSet is backed by a HashMap (hash table), has no guaranteed order, provides O(1) average operations, and allows one null element. Use TreeSet when sorted order or range queries are needed; use HashSet for pure fast membership testing.

items.q: Q2. What is the internal data structure of TreeSet?
items.a: TreeSet is internally backed by a TreeMap. Each element added to a TreeSet is stored as a key in the backing TreeMap with a constant dummy Object value (PRESENT). TreeMap is implemented as a Red-Black Tree — a self-balancing BST that maintains O(log n) height by enforcing Red-Black properties through rotations and recoloring during insertions and deletions.

items.q: Q3. Does TreeSet allow null elements? Why?
items.a: No. TreeSet throws NullPointerException when you attempt to add null. This is because TreeSet must compare elements to maintain sorted order. When comparing a null against any element using compareTo() or compare(), a NullPointerException is thrown. Even if the set is empty, adding null fails because TreeSet validates comparability at insert time.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between ceiling(), floor(), higher(), and lower() in TreeSet?
items.a: floor(e) — greatest element ≤ e (includes e). lower(e) — greatest element strictly < e (excludes e). ceiling(e) — smallest element ≥ e (includes e). higher(e) — smallest element strictly > e (excludes e). Memory trick: floor/ceiling include the boundary; lower/higher exclude it. All return null if no matching element exists.

items.q: Q5. What is the difference between headSet(), tailSet(), and subSet()?
items.a: headSet(toElement) returns a live view of elements strictly less than toElement. tailSet(fromElement) returns a live view of elements greater than or equal to fromElement. subSet(from, to) returns a live view of elements where from ≤ e < to. All three return live backed views — modifications to the view affect the original TreeSet and vice versa. NavigableSet versions of these methods accept boolean inclusive flags for full boundary control.

items.q: Q6. How does TreeSet determine duplicate elements?
items.a: TreeSet uses compareTo() (from Comparable) or compare() (from Comparator) — NOT equals() — to determine duplicates. If compareTo() or compare() returns 0, the element is considered a duplicate and is not inserted (add() returns false). This is why you must ensure your compareTo() is consistent with equals() — if two objects that are logically equal return 0 from compareTo(), only one will be stored.

items.q: Q7. What is the time complexity of TreeSet operations?
items.a: All fundamental operations — add(e), remove(e), contains(e), first(), last(), ceiling(e), floor(e), higher(e), lower(e), pollFirst(), pollLast() — run in O(log n) time. headSet(), tailSet(), subSet() return live views in O(1) time (they just store boundary references). Iterating the entire set is O(n). The O(log n) guarantee is unconditional — no hash collisions, no worst-case degradation.

items.q: Q8. Is TreeSet thread-safe? What is the alternative?
items.a: No, TreeSet is not thread-safe. Concurrent modification can corrupt the Red-Black Tree structure. The best thread-safe alternative for a sorted set is ConcurrentSkipListSet (java.util.concurrent) — it provides lock-free thread safety, maintains sorted order, and has O(log n) operations. You can also wrap with Collections.synchronizedSortedSet(new TreeSet<>()) but must manually synchronize during iteration.

items.q: Q9. What happens when you add an object to TreeSet whose class does not implement Comparable and no Comparator is provided?
items.a: A ClassCastException is thrown at runtime when the second element is added (not the first, because the first element has nothing to compare against). The JVM tries to cast the object to Comparable to call compareTo(), and if the class doesn't implement it, ClassCastException is thrown. Always ensure elements either implement Comparable or a Comparator is provided at TreeSet construction.

items.q: Q10. How does Java 21 improve TreeSet with SequencedSet?
items.a: Java 21 (JEP 431) made TreeSet implement SequencedSet, adding getFirst() (= first()), getLast() (= last()), removeFirst() (= pollFirst()), removeLast() (= pollLast()), and reversed() (= descendingSet()) as standard API. addFirst() and addLast() throw UnsupportedOperationException because TreeSet controls its own order. The main benefit is API uniformity — TreeSet now shares a common interface with List and Deque for first/last operations.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of TreeSet with these practice questions — from basic output prediction to real-world design challenges. Try answering before revealing each answer.

items.a: [Banana, Cherry, apple, banana]. TreeSet sorts Strings lexicographically using Unicode values. Uppercase letters (A-Z, codes 65-90) come before lowercase (a-z, codes 97-122). So the order is: Banana (B=66) → Cherry (C=67) → apple (a=97) → banana (b=98). Note that 'Banana' and 'banana' are NOT duplicates — compareTo() is case-sensitive and returns non-zero.

Line 1: [20, 30, 40] — subSet(20, true, 40, true) means both boundaries are inclusive, so elements where 20 ≤ e ≤ 40. Line 2: [30] — subSet(20, false, 40, false) means both boundaries are exclusive, so elements where 20 < e < 40. Only 30 qualifies.

items.q: 3. A TreeSet<Integer> contains {5, 10, 15, 20, 25}. What does ceiling(15), floor(15), higher(15), lower(15) return?
items.a: ceiling(15) = 15 (smallest element ≥ 15, includes 15 itself). floor(15) = 15 (greatest element ≤ 15, includes 15 itself). higher(15) = 20 (smallest element strictly > 15, excludes 15). lower(15) = 10 (greatest element strictly < 15, excludes 15). When the exact value is present: ceiling and floor return it; higher and lower skip it.

items.q: 4. What exception does TreeSet<Integer> ts = new TreeSet<>(); ts.add(null); throw? Why?
items.a: NullPointerException. TreeSet must compare elements to place them in the correct sorted position using compareTo(). When comparing null using Integer's compareTo(null), a NullPointerException is thrown. TreeSet does not allow null elements for this reason. HashSet and LinkedHashSet allow one null because they use hashCode() (null returns 0) rather than comparison.

items.q: 5. You have a TreeSet sorted by natural order. You call pollFirst() and pollLast() alternately until the set is empty. What is the order of elements retrieved for set {3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6}?
items.a: TreeSet removes duplicate 1, so the sorted set is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9}. Alternating pollFirst/pollLast: pollFirst()=1, pollLast()=9, pollFirst()=2, pollLast()=6, pollFirst()=3, pollLast()=5, pollFirst()=4 (set now empty). Order: 1, 9, 2, 6, 3, 5, 4.

ClassCastException is thrown when adding the second element (42). TreeSet has no Comparator, so it uses natural ordering. When adding Integer 42, TreeSet tries to compare it with the existing String 'Hello' by casting to Comparable and calling compareTo(). A String is not comparable to an Integer, so ClassCastException: class java.lang.String cannot be cast to class java.lang.Integer. Note: adding the first element alone never throws — comparison requires at least two elements.

items.q: 7. Design a solution: Given a list of timestamps (as long values), find all events that occurred between two given timestamps (inclusive) using TreeSet.
items.a: TreeSet<Long> events = new TreeSet<>(timestamps); SortedSet<Long> range = events.subSet(startTime, true, endTime, true); This returns a live backed view of all events where startTime ≤ event ≤ endTime in O(log n) time to find boundaries, then O(k) to iterate k results. This is far more efficient than filtering a list with a for-loop (O(n)) and demonstrates why TreeSet is the right tool for time-window queries.

items.q: 8. Are headSet(), tailSet(), and subSet() views or copies? What happens if you modify the original set while holding a view reference?
items.a: They return live backed views — not copies. The view and the original TreeSet share the same underlying Red-Black Tree. Modifications to the original are instantly visible in the view, and modifications to the view (within its bounds) are instantly applied to the original. Attempting to add an element to a view that falls outside the view's boundary throws IllegalArgumentException — the view enforces its range constraint.

blocks.text: TreeSet is one of Java's most powerful and expressive collection classes — but only when used for the right problems. Its combination of guaranteed sorted order, efficient range views, and NavigableSet proximity queries makes it the ideal choice for a specific category of problems that no other Java collection can solve as elegantly.

Problems involving sorted windows, nearest neighbors, and range frequency counting are naturally solved by TreeSet.

TreeSet mastery signals strong data-structures knowledge. The developer who reaches for TreeSet when the problem calls for it — and knows exactly which NavigableSet method to use — writes code that is not only correct but measurably faster and cleaner than naive alternatives. ☕
